title: NASSCOM Chief: Green Card Curbs Will Push More Work to India's Talent Base
excerpt: In an exclusive interview, NASSCOM chairperson Srikanth Velamakanni says the US PERM suspension of eight tech firms won't hurt Indian IT's bottom line — and argues that when talent can't move, work will move to where the talent is.
body:
• The Trump administration's October 8 suspension freezes new and pending PERM green-card filings at eight companies: Microsoft, Adobe, TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant and Capgemini.
  • In an exclusive NDTV interview, NASSCOM chairperson Srikanth Velamakanni said the fraud allegations against the firms remain unproven, called due process essential, and argued the curbs will not dent Indian IT revenue or profitability in the short to medium term.
  • If you are an H-1B worker at one of the eight companies with a PERM case in the pipeline, your filing is frozen — not cancelled — and H-1B visas themselves are untouched. Velamakanni says Indian IT firms have steadily reduced H-1B dependence for years, so immediate job impacts should be limited.
  • His broader pitch: when workers cannot move, work and capital move to where the talent is — and artificial intelligence is making it cheaper than ever to build a business from India.

The Industry Pushes Back

NASSCOM chairperson Srikanth Velamakanni told NDTV the October 8 suspension of green-card processing at eight major technology companies will not significantly affect Indian IT firms' revenue or profitability in the short to medium term — and could accelerate a shift of work and capital toward India's talent base.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=BccPiTNvPzE

The Trump administration announced on October 8 that it would stop accepting or processing new and pending permanent labour certification applications involving eight companies: Microsoft, Adobe and six IT services firms with deep India ties — Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant and Capgemini. US Vice President JD Vance accused the companies of misusing H-1B visas and the green-card process to replace American workers with what he called "foreign indentured servants," and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the firms alone had sought nearly three million foreign workers since 2009.

"When labour is not able to move to where the work is, the work will move to where the labour is."

— Srikanth Velamakanni, NASSCOM Chairperson

Context & Background

The action targets the PERM program — the Department of Labor process that begins most employment-based green cards. It freezes the H-1B-to-green-card transition at the named companies; H-1B visas themselves are untouched, a distinction Velamakanni was careful to underline.

The suspension followed an investigation by an anti-fraud task force chaired by Vance, which alleged that Microsoft laid off roughly 6,000 American workers last year while employing 6,300 non-citizens brought in on H-1B visas. Microsoft has pushed back: spokeswoman Kate Frischmann said the vast majority of its US employees are American citizens, and that of roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it filed last fiscal year, 80 percent were extensions or status changes for existing employees, not new arrivals.

NASSCOM's own October 8 statement frames its response: immigration and skilled talent mobility are distinct issues, Indian technology companies have spent years reducing H-1B dependence while expanding local hiring in the US, and the number of employees transitioning from H-1B to permanent residency through PERM was relatively limited.

Impact & Analysis

For the Indian IT services majors, the argument is arithmetic. TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant and Capgemini have spent a decade localizing their US workforces and lowering their visa dependence. If the PERM channel freezes only a thin pipeline of green-card conversions, the near-term P&L hit is, as he put it, unlikely to be significant.

The sharper question is reputational. The administration's rhetoric lands on companies that, in Velamakanni's words, are well-governed and compliant, and whose professionals he called victims of "insulting" remarks. But he also conceded Washington's right to enforce its immigration laws, asking only that unproven allegations not be treated as final findings before due process runs its course.

His broader argument is economic: restrictions on the movement of workers push companies to move jobs to where the talent sits. Indians unable to pursue US permanent residency, he suggested, may instead build businesses at home — a path he says artificial intelligence has made materially easier and cheaper, from product development to raising capital. His message to New Delhi was diplomatic but pointed: keep engaging the US administration and "build win-win pathways for India, for the world," even through occasional rhetoric.

What's Next

The named companies are expected to submit additional information — Microsoft has said it plans to. The suspension's duration, and whether pending PERM applications are ultimately revived or voided, remain unclear. The watch items for Indian professionals: whether the freeze expands beyond the eight named firms, how long it lasts, and whether the administration moves from green-card processing to the H-1B program itself — a line Velamakanni insists has not been crossed. NASSCOM's bet is that the industry's decade-long pivot away from visa dependence insulates it. The test of that bet is now underway.
